context_question: What are the primary success goals for Virtual-EDU from NJIT’s perspective—for example, what outcomes should the platform enable for professors, students, and administrators?
answer: From NJIT’s perspective, the main goal is to make online learning feel organized, secure, and easy to use for everyone involved. Professors should be able to teach, communicate, share materials, and manage class activities without relying on scattered tools, and students should be able to participate, collaborate, and access course content reliably from anywhere. For administrators, the platform should make it straightforward to manage users, courses, and the overall environment while keeping the system secure and under control.

context_question: What authentication and access-control requirements should Virtual-EDU enforce for professors, students, and administrators—for example, how users log in, how roles and permissions are assigned, and what actions each role should or should not be allowed to perform?
answer: It should require individual user accounts, and I’d expect login to be tied to NJIT credentials or some other centrally managed authentication rather than shared accounts. Roles would need to be assigned by administration, with professors, students, and admins each seeing only what they’re supposed to see based on course enrollment and job function. Professors should manage their own classes and materials, students should only access the courses they’re enrolled in and participate there, and administrators should have broader management access but still with auditability and restrictions where appropriate.

context_question: What are the key business rules and course lifecycle requirements for Virtual-EDU—for example, how courses are created, approved, opened, closed, archived, and who is allowed to perform each action?
answer: I’d expect courses to be created and maintained by administrators, or at least provisioned by them even if professors help set up the content. There should be a clear lifecycle so a course can be opened for enrollment and activity at the start of a term, then closed when the term ends, and archived afterward so records and materials remain available as needed but the course is no longer actively used. I’m not sure yet whether professors should be allowed to request changes or create course shells directly, so that would need to be confirmed with NJIT’s policy.

context_question: What communication channels should Virtual-EDU support for professors, students, and administrators—such as announcements, direct messaging, group chat, discussion forums, email notifications, or live video/audio sessions—and are there any requirements for when each channel should be used?
answer: At minimum, I’d expect announcements for class-wide messages, direct messaging for one-on-one communication, and group communication for team work or class discussions. Email notifications should probably be used for important alerts like new announcements, assignment deadlines, or messages when users are not actively in the system. Live video or audio sessions would be important for lectures or office hours, but I’d need to confirm whether Virtual-EDU is supposed to host those natively or just integrate with an existing tool.

context_question: For live video or audio sessions such as lectures and office hours, should Virtual-EDU provide the conferencing capability natively within the platform, or should it integrate with an existing external tool—and if integration is preferred, which tool(s) and what level of integration are expected?
answer: My assumption would be that integration is preferred unless NJIT specifically wants to replace an existing conferencing solution, because that’s usually faster and less disruptive for faculty and students. I don’t know which tool NJIT would want to standardize on, so that would need to be confirmed, but the level of integration should at least let users launch a session from the course page and see the meeting link or schedule in context. If we do use an external tool, it should feel embedded enough that professors can schedule sessions and students can join without a lot of extra steps.

context_question: Should Virtual-EDU include discussion forums and assignment/deadline management, and if so, what specific behaviors and rules should each support—for example, forum structure and moderation, assignment creation and submission, deadline handling, late work, and any grading or notification expectations?
answer: Yes, I would expect both discussion forums and assignment management to be part of the platform. Forums should probably be organized by course and topic, with professors able to moderate or remove inappropriate content, and students able to post and reply within their enrolled courses. Assignments should let professors post work with deadlines, students submit files or text responses, and the system should handle due dates, late submissions, and notify users about upcoming deadlines or newly posted work.

context_question: Should Virtual-EDU include a gradebook and assessment tracking, and if so, what should it record and how should grades be calculated and displayed—for example, who can enter or edit grades, whether students can see grades immediately or only after release, and whether the system should support weighted categories, drops, curves, or other calculation rules?
answer: Yes, I’d expect a gradebook to be included, because that’s a core part of a course portal. Professors should be able to enter and edit grades for their own courses, while students should only be able to view their own results, and whether grades appear immediately or only after release may need to be configurable by the professor. For the calculation rules, I know weighted categories are important, but I’m not sure yet whether NJIT wants drops, curves, or other special grading logic built in, so that would need to be verified.

context_question: For grading and assignment deadlines in Virtual-EDU, are there any special rules NJIT wants beyond weighted categories—for example grade drops, curves, extra credit, late-submission grace periods, or other deadline exceptions—and if so, how should those rules work?
answer: I’m not aware of any NJIT-wide special grading rules beyond the basic weighted categories, and I wouldn’t want to assume drops or curves are standard. Extra credit and late work grace periods seem like the kinds of things professors might want to control per course or per assignment, but that would need confirmation. If those are supported, they should probably be configurable by the instructor rather than hard-coded into the system.

context_question: For live video/audio sessions and other real-time activities in Virtual-EDU, what scale and performance expectations should the system meet—for example, how many concurrent users or sessions per course, what response or latency targets are acceptable, and are there peak-load periods or other capacity constraints NJIT wants the platform to handle?
answer: I don’t have exact numbers for concurrent users or session capacity, so those limits would need to be confirmed with NJIT and whatever conferencing tool we use. My expectation is that the system should support normal class sizes without noticeable delay and remain usable during peak times like the start of term, exam periods, and scheduled lecture hours. For live sessions, low latency and stable joining should be treated as important, but the precise performance targets aren’t something I can give you yet.

context_question: What grading options should instructors be able to configure per course or assignment in Virtual-EDU—for example extra credit, late-work grace periods, drops, curves, or other special grading rules—and how should each option work?
answer: Instructors should at least be able to configure extra credit and some kind of late-work handling per assignment or course, because those are common teaching needs. I would also expect them to control whether an assignment can be dropped from the final grade, but I’m not sure about automatic curves, since that may be more of a departmental policy than a system feature. The exact behavior for each option should probably be course-specific and left to the instructor unless NJIT wants a standard policy enforced across the platform.

context_question: Should Virtual-EDU be designed with any specific priorities for mobile use and accessibility—for example, must it work well on phones and tablets, support offline or low-connectivity access, or meet any accessibility standards such as WCAG or NJIT compliance requirements?
answer: Yes, I’d consider mobile support important, because students and professors will likely use phones or tablets at least some of the time. I’m not sure about offline access, and I wouldn’t assume that unless NJIT specifically asks for it, but the platform should handle low-connectivity situations as gracefully as possible. Accessibility should absolutely be a priority, and I’d expect us to align with WCAG and any NJIT accessibility requirements once those are confirmed.

context_question: For course materials and student submissions in Virtual-EDU, what should the system retain and for how long—for example, should it keep version history for edited files, and are there specific file types, size limits, virus/malware checks, or other submission restrictions that need to be enforced?
answer: I’d expect the system to retain course materials and submitted assignments for at least the duration of the course, and probably longer if NJIT wants records kept for audit or academic reference. Version history would be useful for edited files, especially for collaborative documents or revised submissions, but I’m not sure whether that has to be kept indefinitely. File type limits, size limits, and malware scanning should definitely be enforced, though the exact allowed formats and thresholds would need to be set by NJIT or the course instructor.

context_question: For assignment submissions in Virtual-EDU, which file types should be allowed or blocked, what size limits should apply, and how should malware/security scanning be handled—for example, should the rules be standardized by NJIT, configurable by instructors per course, or both?
answer: I’d lean toward a standard NJIT baseline for allowed file types, size limits, and malware scanning, with instructors able to tighten restrictions if needed for a specific course. I’d expect common academic formats like PDF, Word, PowerPoint, spreadsheets, images, and maybe source-code files for programming courses to be allowed, while executables and obviously risky file types should be blocked. Malware scanning should happen automatically on upload before the file is made available to others, but the exact size caps are something NJIT would have to define.

answer: That’s pretty important. The system should record timestamps for submissions, grading actions, and feedback so there’s a reliable audit trail, especially when deadlines or disputes come up. It should also clearly mark late work, resubmissions, and version history so professors and students can see exactly what was turned in and when.

context_question: You mentioned the importance of tracking timestamps and marking late or resubmissions clearly for grading history. Could you describe how timely feedback delivery should be handled in Virtual-EDU? For example, are there expectations for notifying students immediately when feedback is posted, or any specific workflows professors should follow to ensure feedback is both prompt and clear?
answer: Yes, students should be notified when feedback is posted, ideally right away through the platform, and possibly by email as well if that’s enabled. I’d expect professors to be able to release feedback when they’re ready, either for the whole class or for individual students, and the workflow should make it clear whether grades are still provisional. The key expectation is that feedback is visible quickly, easy to find, and tied directly to the assignment or submission it refers to.

context_question: Now that we’ve covered feedback workflows, I’d like to ask about the transition to Virtual-EDU. Does NJIT expect to migrate existing course materials, user data, or communications from current tools into the new platform? If so, could you describe what kinds of data or content should be migrated and any key considerations or challenges you foresee in that migration process?
answer: Yes, there should be migration support for at least the core course materials and user accounts, and possibly some historical course content depending on what NJIT decides to carry forward. Things like syllabi, documents, assignment descriptions, grades, and basic enrollment data are likely candidates, but I’m not sure whether old messages or discussion archives need to come over in every case. A big concern would be preserving structure and access permissions correctly, because the migrated data has to land in the right course spaces without exposing anything to the wrong users.

context_question: That makes a lot of sense, especially about preserving structure and access controls during migration. Could you share how NJIT envisions the actual migration process? For example, are there expectations around timing, automation, validation steps, or how to handle any issues that come up during migration?
answer: I’d expect migration to be mostly automated where possible, with a structured cutover plan so it doesn’t interfere too much with the semester schedule. Validation is important, so NJIT would likely want checks to confirm files, enrollments, and permissions moved correctly before going live. If problems come up, the process should log them clearly and let administrators retry or correct specific items rather than failing the entire migration.

context_question: Thanks for explaining the migration process so clearly. To build on that, could you describe NJIT’s expectations around data conversion during migration? For example, are there specific file formats, metadata standards, or transformation rules that Virtual-EDU should support to ensure course materials and assignments import correctly and maintain integrity?
answer: We’d want Virtual-EDU to handle the common academic file types without breaking them, like PDF, Word documents, spreadsheets, images, and standard video or audio formats if those are being used. Metadata is important too, especially course name, term, owner, due dates, and permission info, because that’s what keeps the content organized and usable after import. I don’t know that there’s a single NJIT-wide standard already decided for every source system, but the conversion should preserve as much original structure and context as possible and flag anything it can’t map cleanly.

context_question: Thanks for sharing those details on data formats and metadata. To get a fuller picture, could you describe NJIT’s overall plans or expectations for migrating existing course data and user information into Virtual-EDU? Are there particular challenges or priorities around the migration process that we should be aware of to ensure a smooth transition?
answer: The main priority is a smooth transition with minimal disruption to active classes, so course data and user information need to come across accurately and on time. We’d want the migration to preserve identity relationships, enrollments, permissions, and key content so instructors don’t have to rebuild courses from scratch. The biggest challenges are usually data quality, mismatched formats between old tools and the new platform, and making sure nothing sensitive is exposed during the move.

context_question: Thanks for outlining those migration priorities and challenges. To help us design the migration process effectively, could you share more about NJIT’s expectations for automation and validation during migration? For example, how much manual intervention is acceptable, what kinds of validation checks are critical before going live, and how should errors or mismatches be handled to minimize disruption?
answer: We’d want as much of the migration as possible to be automated so staff aren’t spending a lot of time doing manual cleanup. Manual intervention should really be limited to exceptions, like bad source data, ambiguous mappings, or anything that fails validation. Before going live, the critical checks are that users are matched correctly, enrollments and permissions are right, course materials open properly, and no content or grades were lost or duplicated. If there are errors or mismatches, they should be reported clearly, queued for review, and fixable in a targeted way without restarting the entire migration.

context_question: To understand how Virtual-EDU should support grading and feedback, could you describe NJIT’s expectations for timely feedback delivery workflows? For example, what key steps should professors follow to release feedback, and how should students be notified to ensure they become promptly aware and clearly understand their results?
answer: Professors should be able to enter feedback, review it, and then explicitly publish or release it when they’re ready. Once it’s released, students should get a clear notification inside the platform, and ideally an email alert too if that’s part of the setup. The feedback view should make it obvious which assignment it belongs to, whether the grade is final or still provisional, and any comments or rubric details should be easy for students to understand.

context_question: That sounds like a solid approach to feedback release and notification. To get a clearer picture, could you walk me through the typical workflow professors would follow from entering feedback to publishing it? For example, are there any review or approval steps, options to release feedback in batches or individually, or ways to handle provisional grades? Also, how should the system handle notifications to ensure students don’t miss important updates?
answer: Typically, the professor would enter grades and comments, save them as draft or provisional, and then do a final review before publishing. We’d want support for releasing feedback either one student at a time or in batches for the whole class, since both patterns happen depending on the assignment. For provisional grades, the system should clearly label them as not final and avoid triggering the same level of notification as a confirmed release unless the professor intends that.

context_question: That’s very helpful detail on the feedback workflow and provisional grades. To make sure students don’t miss important feedback, how does NJIT envision the notification process working? For example, should the system send reminders or escalate alerts if students don’t view their feedback within a certain timeframe? Are there preferred channels or timing for these notifications to keep students promptly informed without overwhelming them?
answer: We’d want the initial notification to go out right when feedback is released, and that should be enough in most cases. Email and an in-system alert are the main channels I’d expect, but I’m not sure NJIT would want a lot of escalation beyond that unless it’s for something urgent like a deadline or a required correction. Reminders could be useful, but they should be configurable so we don’t end up spamming students for every grade update.

context_question: Thanks for clarifying the notification preferences. To help us anticipate potential challenges, have there been any past or anticipated situations where requirements around feedback release timing, notification frequency, or privacy created conflicts or trade-offs for NJIT? For example, balancing timely alerts with avoiding notification overload or managing provisional versus final grades?
answer: Yes, that balance is definitely a concern. Professors want students to see updates quickly, but too many alerts can become noise, especially in courses with lots of small assignments. Privacy is the other issue, since provisional grades or sensitive feedback shouldn’t be exposed too broadly, so we’d need controls that let instructors choose what gets released, to whom, and when.

context_question: It’s great to hear about the need for flexible controls to balance timely feedback and privacy. Could you share any specific examples or scenarios where NJIT has faced or anticipates conflicts between releasing feedback quickly and protecting sensitive information? For instance, how have professors or administrators handled situations where provisional grades or sensitive comments needed careful timing or selective visibility?
answer: A common case is when a professor has grades ready but wants to hold them until after the whole class has been reviewed, so nobody sees partial results too early. Another situation is when comments include sensitive academic concerns, and those need to stay visible only to the student and instructor, not in any broader class view. In those cases, the expectation is that the system supports selective release and clear visibility settings so instructors can control exactly when and how the information appears.

context_question: Thanks for those examples—they really highlight the need for precise control over feedback visibility. Could you share any specific situations NJIT has encountered where the timing or selective release of feedback led to conflicts or challenges? For instance, how have professors or administrators managed cases where releasing partial grades early caused issues, or where sensitive comments needed extra protection? Understanding these real-world scenarios will help us design better support for those trade-offs.
answer: One challenge is when some students get feedback early because their work was graded first, and others notice the difference and think the instructor is favoring certain people. That usually pushes professors to wait and release everything together, or at least keep draft statuses hidden until the full set is ready. For sensitive comments, the main concern is accidental exposure through class lists, shared views, or notifications, so the system needs very tight per-student visibility and confirmation before anything is published.

context_question: Could you describe specific examples or scenarios where NJIT has experienced conflicts between the need to release feedback quickly and the need to protect sensitive or provisional information? How have professors or administrators managed these situations so far?
answer: A typical example is when an instructor finishes grading a subset of submissions early, but wants to wait because the comments include corrections or concerns that should be handled consistently across the whole class. In practice, they usually keep everything in draft until the full review is done, then release it all at once to avoid confusion and complaints. For anything sensitive, the professor may share it directly with the individual student and avoid putting it in any broader announcement or class-visible context.

context_question: That makes sense, especially the need to keep draft feedback hidden until everything is ready. Looking ahead, are there any open issues or unresolved questions at NJIT about how to balance notification frequency with privacy controls? For example, are there any policy or technical uncertainties that might affect how these features get prioritized or implemented in Virtual-EDU?
answer: Yes, there are still some open questions around how much control instructors should have versus how much should be standardized for consistency across courses. We also haven’t fully settled what counts as a required notification versus an optional reminder, especially when privacy is involved and we don’t want repeated alerts exposing too much detail. I’d say the policy side is still being worked out, so that could affect whether the system leans toward simple default behavior or more configurable options.

context_question: Given the open questions around notification frequency and privacy, could you describe how NJIT envisions escalation or reminder policies for feedback notifications? For example, should the system send repeated reminders if students don’t view feedback promptly, or escalate alerts to professors or administrators? How configurable should these policies be to balance timely awareness without causing notification fatigue?
answer: I think the default should be one initial notification and maybe a single reminder after a reasonable delay, but not an aggressive chain of alerts. Escalating to professors or administrators would probably only make sense for truly time-sensitive items, not routine feedback, because that could create a lot of unnecessary overhead. Ideally, the reminder policy should be configurable at the course level or by instructors, with NJIT setting a broad standard so students aren’t flooded differently in every class.

context_question: That approach to a default plus configurable reminders sounds like a good balance. Could you describe how NJIT envisions the details of these escalation and reminder policies working? For example, what specific triggers should cause reminders to be sent, who should receive escalations if feedback remains unacknowledged, and how much flexibility should professors or administrators have to customize these settings within their courses?
answer: A reminder should probably be triggered only after feedback has been posted and the student hasn’t opened it within a set window, maybe a day or two for ordinary items. If something is truly urgent, like a deadline-related correction or a required academic notice, then an escalation could go to the professor first, not straight to an administrator. Professors should have some flexibility to adjust timing within NJIT’s limits, but administrators would likely want guardrails so people can’t create constant alerts or hide important notices too long.

context_question: Thanks for outlining those key points on timing and escalation recipients. To get a clearer picture, could you walk me through how NJIT envisions these escalation and reminder policies working in practice? For example, what specific events or triggers should prompt reminders or escalations, who exactly should receive these alerts at each stage, and how much flexibility should professors or administrators have to customize these settings within their courses or roles?
answer: In practice, I’d expect a reminder to go out when feedback is posted, then another only if it stays unread past a course-defined window, and only for items marked as important or time-sensitive. If it still isn’t acknowledged, the next alert would usually go to the professor or course staff, since they are the ones who can decide whether follow-up is needed. Professors should be able to tune the timing a bit for their courses, but NJIT would probably want administrators to set limits on minimum and maximum delays, plus what kinds of messages are allowed to escalate at all.

context_question: Building on what you shared about escalation policies, could you describe how NJIT currently handles situations where students repeatedly ignore feedback notifications? Are there any manual or automated escalation steps in place, and how well have those worked so far?
answer: Right now, as far as I know, it’s mostly handled manually by the instructor. If a student seems to be ignoring important feedback, the professor might follow up directly by email or in class, but I don’t believe there’s a formal automated escalation process in place today. That works okay for small classes, but it can get messy when there are many students or when the feedback is time-sensitive.

context_question: Thanks for sharing how manual follow-up is currently done. Building on that, what concerns or reservations have professors and administrators expressed about introducing automated escalation alerts? How might these concerns shape the way Virtual-EDU designs escalation and reminder features to ensure they are effective but not overwhelming or intrusive?
answer: The biggest concern is that automated escalations could feel too invasive if they keep alerting students or staff over something minor. Professors also worry that it could create extra noise for them if they start getting notified about every unread comment instead of just the important ones. That would probably push Virtual-EDU toward clear defaults, limited escalation paths, and controls that let instructors decide what is worth chasing without turning the system into a constant reminder machine.

context_question: That makes a lot of sense, keeping escalation sensible and non-intrusive is key. Building on that, could you share how NJIT currently handles situations where students repeatedly ignore feedback notifications? Are there any manual or automated escalation steps in place today, and how effective have those been in practice?
answer: It’s still mostly a manual process today. If a student keeps missing feedback, the professor or TA usually reaches out directly, and in some cases they may mention it during office hours or class. That can be effective when the class is small, but it’s inconsistent and depends a lot on the instructor’s follow-up habits, so it doesn’t scale very well.

context_question: Thanks for sharing how manual follow-up works today. Looking ahead, how does NJIT envision balancing the flexibility professors have to customize escalation and reminder settings with the need for administrative governance? For example, how might NJIT prevent misuse or ensure students have a consistent notification experience across different courses while still allowing instructors some control?
answer: I think NJIT would want a central policy that sets the boundaries, and then instructors can work inside those boundaries for their own courses. So professors might choose timing within a range, but they shouldn’t be able to turn off required notices or set reminders so aggressively that students get spammed. To keep the experience consistent, administrators would probably need visibility into the settings and the ability to override them if a course configuration starts causing problems.

context_question: That makes sense about setting boundaries and giving instructors some room to adjust within them. Looking further, does NJIT envision any policies or mechanisms for handling situations where students repeatedly ignore urgent feedback even after reminders and escalations? For example, might academic advisors or other support roles get involved beyond professors and administrators? How would those extended escalation paths work in practice?
answer: Yes, for repeated non-response on something truly urgent, I could see the matter moving beyond the professor to a department contact or academic advisor. That would probably only happen for defined cases, like major assignment risk, attendance issues, or a pattern that suggests the student may need support rather than just another reminder. I’m not sure NJIT has a formal policy for that yet, but if it exists it would need to be tightly controlled so those extra escalations are rare and clearly justified.

context_question: That makes sense about involving advisors or department contacts only in rare, well-justified cases. Shifting gears a bit, how does NJIT envision balancing the flexibility professors have to customize escalation and reminder settings with the need for administrative governance? For example, how might NJIT prevent misuse or ensure students have a consistent notification experience across different courses while still allowing instructors some control?
answer: I’d expect NJIT to define a standard policy at the institution level, then let instructors adjust only certain parts like reminder frequency or who gets copied, within approved limits. Administrators would need to keep an eye on those settings, especially if a course starts sending too many alerts or using unusual escalation paths, and they’d have the authority to reset things back to the standard behavior. The main goal would be to keep the student experience predictable across courses while still giving instructors enough control to manage their own classes effectively.

context_question: What would you say are the main goals and expected classroom experience for distance learning in this context?
answer: The main goal is to make remote learning feel organized, secure, and close to a real classroom experience. We want professors and students to be able to communicate easily, share course materials, work together on assignments, and take part in class activities without a lot of friction. It should feel natural for an enrolled student to join a course, follow along, interact, and get support from the instructor and classmates online.

context_question: What are the main pain points or frustrations students and instructors face in the current online instruction setup that this new experience should specifically address?
answer: The biggest issues are usually scattered communication, trouble finding the right materials, and too many separate tools that don’t work together well. Instructors also struggle with managing participation and keeping everyone engaged, while students can feel disconnected or unsure where to go for updates, assignments, or help. Security and access control are also important, because we need to make sure only enrolled users are in the course environment.

context_question: When you think about moving from any existing learning tools or repositories into this new environment, what would the migration need to accomplish for instructors and students in practice, and what kinds of content or workflows would need to carry over to avoid disrupting courses?
answer: Migration would need to bring over the core course content and the active course structure so classes can keep running without restarting from scratch. In practice, that means materials like documents, slides, assignments, announcements, and maybe discussion history or shared resources, if those exist, along with enrolled users and their course memberships. We’d also want the usual workflows to carry over, such as submitting assignments, posting updates, and accessing the same course spaces, so instructors and students don’t lose momentum.

context_question: Before go-live, are there any specific data conversion, cleansing, or mapping rules you’d want applied to migrated course records or user memberships, such as handling duplicates, incomplete entries, or legacy formats?
answer: Yes, we’d want duplicates cleaned up and incomplete records flagged before anything is loaded, especially for user accounts and course enrollments. Legacy formats would need to be mapped into the new structure in a consistent way, and anything ambiguous should be reviewed instead of guessed at, because access and course membership have to be accurate. If some records can’t be converted cleanly, I’d expect them to be reported so the team can decide whether to correct them manually or leave them out.

context_question: Now that the migration side is clearer, when you think about the initial Virtual-EDU release, what would you want to make sure is included first so it delivers the most value to students and instructors right away, and what could wait for a later phase?
answer: For the first release, I’d want the basics fully working: secure login, course enrollment and access control, course pages, file sharing, communication between instructors and students, and the ability to post and submit course activities. Those are the pieces that make the environment useful on day one. Things like advanced analytics, extra integrations, and more polished collaboration features could probably come later if needed.

context_question: Are there any prerequisites or delivery dependencies among those first-release features that would affect the order you’d want them built or launched?
answer: Yes, security and user access need to come first, because nothing else should be available until we know the right people are getting into the right courses. After that, the course structure and enrollment setup have to be in place before file sharing and class activities can really work properly. Communication can come alongside that, but it still depends on having the user and course context established first.

context_question: What outcomes or situations would tell you that the first release is acceptable, and are there any decisions you still need to make about how to handle cases where access, enrollment, or class activity setup doesn’t go as expected?
answer: We’d consider the first release acceptable if instructors can run a class and students can join, communicate, access materials, and complete activities without major issues. It should be stable, secure, and usable enough that people don’t need workarounds for the basic teaching flow. For edge cases like failed enrollment or access problems, I know we’ll need a clear policy, but I’d want to confirm with the team whether those should be handled automatically, queued for review, or sent to an administrator for correction.

context_question: Are there any situations where you’d want to prioritize security over convenience, or usability over strict controls, even if that means some users have a slightly harder time getting in or completing tasks?
answer: Yes, security has to win in any situation where there’s a risk of unauthorized access, especially around course membership, grades, or private communication. We’d rather make a legitimate user take one extra step than let the wrong person into a class or shared material. At the same time, for routine class tasks, we’d want the system to stay as simple as possible so students and instructors can actually use it without friction.

context_question: In the NJIT course and online participation context, can you walk me through the main ways you expect students and instructors to use the system during a typical class, including any important situations where access or participation might need to work differently?
answer: A typical class would start with students and instructors logging in, going to their course space, and seeing the materials, announcements, and activities for that course. Instructors would post content, share files, communicate with the class or with individual students, and set up assignments or participation activities, while students would review materials, ask questions, submit work, and join group discussions. Access might need to work differently for guest speakers, late add/drop changes, or special permission cases, but I’d want those handled in a controlled way so the normal class flow stays secure.

context_question: Besides the standard classroom flow you described, what course formats or teaching scenarios does NJIT need Virtual-EDU to support?
answer: We definitely need it to support more than just a normal lecture course. Lab sections, discussion-based classes, and project or team-based courses are all likely, and some instructors may want to run hybrid classes where part of the work is online and part is in person. I’m not sure yet whether there are special cases like cross-listed courses or guest instructor access, but those are the kinds of scenarios we should verify.

context_question: About how many students, course sections, and concurrently active users do you expect Virtual-EDU to support during a typical term, and do you anticipate any larger peak loads during registration, exams, or other busy periods?
answer: I don’t have exact numbers yet, so I’d need to confirm that with NJIT enrollment data and whoever owns the academic systems. My expectation is that normal daily use will be much lower than peak usage, but registration periods, exam weeks, and the start of term will drive noticeable spikes. We should plan for those busy windows so the system stays responsive even when many students are logging in at the same time.

context_question: Are there any special course scenarios at NJIT, such as cross-listed classes, guest instructors, or similar exceptions, that Virtual-EDU needs to handle differently from a standard course?
answer: Yes, I would expect at least some of those cases, especially cross-listed courses and guest instructors. Cross-listed classes would need to behave like one shared course space even if students are coming from different departments, and guest instructors would likely need limited access rather than full control. I’d want to confirm the exact rules for those exceptions before locking down the design.

context_question: When you think about how NJIT should refer to courses, groups, and learning activities in Virtual-EDU, what terms or distinctions matter most in the real academic workflows it needs to support?
answer: The main distinction is between the official course section and the smaller groups inside it, because instructors may want to address the whole class or just a lab or project team. Learning activities should also be clearly separate from content, since something like an assignment, quiz, or discussion has different handling than a file or announcement. I’d also want the terminology to match what NJIT faculty and students already use, so it feels familiar instead of forcing new labels.

context_question: When NJIT needs to distinguish between a whole course section, a smaller student cohort like a lab or project team, and an instructor-managed space for activities, what naming conventions or labels should Virtual-EDU use, and are there any cases where the same group needs to be referred to differently?
answer: I’d keep the official term as the course section, since that’s the enrolled class tied to NJIT records. For smaller cohorts, labels like lab group, project team, or discussion group would make sense depending on the teaching context, and the system should let the instructor name them in a way that fits the course. In some cases the same group might be referred to both by its functional name and by its section affiliation, especially when multiple sections share a resource or activity space.

context_question: For the first release, how should Virtual-EDU handle enrollment or access problems when a student can’t get into the right course section or a student group—should those cases be corrected automatically, queued for review, or sent to an administrator?
answer: For the first release, I’d expect those problems to be queued for review rather than corrected automatically. If a student can’t get into the right section or group, the system should flag it clearly and route it to an administrator or support staff member who can verify the record and fix it safely. Automatic correction sounds risky at this stage unless the rule is very simple and we’re completely confident in the source data.

context_question: What specific controls should administrators have over users, courses, and permissions in Virtual-EDU beyond reviewing and fixing enrollment issues?
answer: Administrators should be able to create, deactivate, and update user accounts, and assign people to the right roles like student, instructor, TA, or guest. They’ll also need to create or manage course shells, control who can access a course or group, and adjust permissions when instructors need extra help or when access has to be restricted. I’d also expect some ability to monitor activity and intervene if there’s a policy or security issue.

context_question: For those lab, discussion, project-based, or hybrid courses, what operational differences should Virtual-EDU support in how sections are set up or managed—for example, separate meeting times, split access, or different activity structures across formats?
answer: Virtual-EDU should support sections that have different meeting patterns, because labs and discussions often run on a separate schedule from the main lecture. It should also allow split access where one group can see only the materials or activities meant for them, especially in project-based or hybrid setups. In practice, the activity structure may vary by format, so the system needs enough flexibility for instructors to organize content, assignments, and group work differently from one course to the next.

context_question: For cross-listed courses, what should happen when one department wants a different access restriction or visibility rule than the others—should the shared course space always follow a single common set of rules, or can there be exceptions by department or role?
answer: For the shared course space, I’d lean toward a single common set of rules so students aren’t getting conflicting access in the same environment. If a department needs a different restriction, that should probably be handled through role-based exceptions or separate subgroups, not by making the whole shared space behave differently. I’d want the system to support exceptions, but only in a controlled way so the overall course stays consistent.

context_question: What kinds of exceptions should the portal allow in a shared course space—for example, by role, subgroup, or specific access rule—and are there any exception types that should not be permitted?
answer: Role-based exceptions are the most important, like letting instructors and TAs see more tools or manage submissions while students have limited access. Subgroup exceptions should also be allowed for things like lab sections, project teams, or accommodated students who need different materials or due dates. I would not want ad hoc exceptions that let a single user bypass the course’s main visibility rules unless there is a formal admin-approved reason, because that gets hard to audit and could create fairness issues.

context_question: When you think about creating a subgroup in Virtual-EDU, what business rules should determine whether it is based on a lab section, project team, accommodation need, or another criterion?
answer: The main rule should be the teaching purpose: if the subgroup is tied to instruction delivery, like a lab or discussion, it should follow the course structure; if it’s for collaboration, then project teams make sense; and if it’s for accessibility or special support, then accommodation-based groups should be allowed. The instructor or admin should choose the subgroup type, but the system should require a clear reason so it’s not just an arbitrary grouping. I’d also expect the subgroup to inherit some permissions from the parent course, unless there’s a specific approved exception.

context_question: When students need to find materials, assignments, updates, or help in one place, what should happen if something is posted only in a subgroup or by a specific role—should it still appear in the main course space, and if so, under what visibility rules?
answer: Yes, if it’s relevant to the whole course it should surface in the main course space, even if it was posted from a subgroup or by a specific role. If it’s meant only for that subgroup, then it should stay hidden from everyone else, but there should still be a clear indication that something exists for the people who have access. The visibility rule should follow the content’s audience, so students only see what applies to them and staff can see the full context.

context_question: When sections meet on different schedules, what practical rules should the system use to keep lecture, lab, and discussion activity organized and visible correctly across the course?
answer: The system should keep the section schedule attached to each activity type, so a lecture, lab, or discussion shows its own meeting time and location or online room. If a student is enrolled in multiple related sections, it should clearly separate what applies to each one and avoid duplicating the same update everywhere unless it is meant to be shared. I’d also want the calendar and reminders to respect the student’s actual section assignments so they only get the activities that affect them.

context_question: When a student’s section assignment changes or they are enrolled in multiple sections for the same course, what rules should determine which calendar entries and reminders are shown, hidden, or updated for them?
answer: The student should only see calendar entries and reminders for the sections they’re currently assigned to, and anything from an old section should drop off once the change is effective. If they’re in multiple sections, the system should show all applicable items, but it should make it obvious which section each one belongs to so they can tell them apart. When a section change happens, reminders tied to that section should update automatically instead of leaving stale notices behind.

context_question: When a section change affects a student’s calendar or reminders, what should happen to items that were already sent or synced—should they be removed, updated in place, or left visible for any reason during the transition?
answer: Already sent reminders probably shouldn’t be erased from the user’s history, because that would be confusing and bad for auditing. But anything still upcoming should be updated in place if the change is known early enough, and if a reminder or calendar item no longer applies, it should disappear from the active view. During the transition, I’d want a short grace period only if needed for sync delays, but not long-term visibility of outdated items.

context_question: When students need to find course updates, assignments, readings, or help, what practical rules should govern how communication and materials are organized so they can quickly tell what applies to them and avoid missing important participation-related information?
answer: The main rule should be that course-wide items are separated from section-specific and subgroup-specific items, and each post or file needs a clear label showing who it applies to. Important participation-related notices, like deadlines, attendance expectations, or discussion requirements, should always be surfaced in the student’s main view if they affect them, with a link back to the detailed section or group context. I’d also want a single “priority” or “important” flag for urgent updates so students don’t miss something just because it was posted in a lower-traffic area.

context_question: What performance expectations should we define for online messaging, file uploads, and activity participation so users know how quickly they should respond, how long uploads may take, and when an activity counts as successfully recorded?
answer: For messaging, I’d expect it to feel near real time during normal use, so sending and receiving should happen within a few seconds at most. File uploads should show progress and be able to handle larger course materials without timing out too easily, though I don’t know the exact size limit yet and would need to confirm that. For activity participation, it should count as recorded as soon as the system confirms the submission or action was received successfully, not just when the student clicks submit.

context_question: Are there any practical limits or special cases for page loads and content delivery—such as slower network conditions, very large pages or files, or first-time access—where it would be acceptable for content to take longer to appear?
answer: Yes, slower loads are acceptable in those cases, especially for large files, rich media, or a first-time access when the system has to initialize everything. In normal day-to-day use, though, the course space should still feel responsive, and content should appear progressively if it can’t load all at once. If the network is weak, it’s more important that the user sees partial content and a clear loading state than a blank screen.

context_question: When instructors or students post messages or shared files within a section or group, what rules should determine who can see them, and under what conditions should something stay private versus being visible to the whole course?
answer: Anything posted in a section or group should stay visible only to the members of that section or group by default. It should become course-wide only if the poster intentionally shares it at that level, or if the instructor has set it as an announcement that everyone needs to see. Private messages between individuals should remain private unless there’s an explicit reason to forward or copy them.

context_question: When someone creates shared content in a course space, what rules should determine who is allowed to post it, edit it later, or remove it?
answer: Instructors should be able to post, edit, and remove course content in their own sections, and administrators should have override access if there’s a support or policy reason. Students should usually only be able to create and edit their own contributions, like discussion posts or uploaded assignments, and they shouldn’t be able to change or delete someone else’s material. If content is shared to a group space, then members of that group may need limited editing rights for collaborative work, but I’d want the instructor to control whether that is allowed.

context_question: When administrators create, deactivate, or change user accounts and roles, what privacy, compliance, or institutional-policy checks should govern when they can view user data, intervene in an account, or override normal access, and are there any cases where those actions should require approval or be limited?
answer: Administrators should only view the user data they need for their job, and anything sensitive should be restricted by role and logged for audit purposes. If they need to intervene in an account or override access, that should be allowed for support, security, or policy enforcement, but not casually, and we should probably limit that to designated admins. I’d expect some actions, like changing roles or deactivating an account, to require approval or at least a second review in special cases, especially if it affects faculty accounts or an active student record.

context_question: For migrated records, what specific rules should we use to decide when a duplicate can be merged automatically versus when it must be left for manual review or excluded, especially for user accounts and course enrollments?
answer: For user accounts, I’d only merge automatically when the match is very strong, like the same institutional ID or a verified email plus matching name and status. If there’s any conflict in identity details, role, or enrollment history, it should go to manual review instead of guessing. Course enrollments should be excluded from auto-merge unless the course code, term, and user identity all line up cleanly, because a bad merge there could put someone in the wrong class or hide a real enrollment.

context_question: What should happen to course records after a course ends or is closed—do they need to be kept indefinitely, archived after a certain period, or removed under any specific conditions?
answer: Course records should definitely be kept for a period of time after the course ends, because faculty and administration may need access for audits, grade disputes, or accreditation purposes. My assumption is that they would be archived rather than deleted in normal cases, and then only removed if there’s a formal retention policy or legal reason to do so. I don’t know the exact retention period yet, so that would need to be confirmed with NJIT policy.

context_question: When a course record is incomplete or has conflicting information, would you want us to exclude it from the system until it can be corrected, or keep it in a limited form for manual correction and review?
answer: Keep it in a limited form for manual correction and review. Excluding it entirely could make it harder to trace what went wrong, especially during migration or reconciliation, so it’s better to preserve the record with flags showing that it needs attention. That way admins can correct it without losing the original information.

context_question: When we migrate course records, what specific retention or archival rules should determine how long they stay accessible, and are there any cases where a course record should be kept longer, restricted, or removed before the normal retention period?
answer: They should stay accessible according to NJIT’s records retention and academic policy, and I’d expect archived access for a defined period rather than open access forever. Certain records, like those tied to grade disputes, audits, accreditation, or legal holds, should be kept longer and possibly restricted to authorized staff only. I don’t know the exact timeframes or any special exceptions offhand, so those would need to be confirmed with the university’s policy team.

context_question: Are there any situations where a one-off access exception should be allowed for a specific person, and if so, what formal approval and audit details would you need before granting it?
answer: Yes, but only in exceptional cases, like troubleshooting a support issue, resolving a grading dispute, or handling an urgent administrative matter. Before granting it, I’d want documented approval from an appropriate supervisor or system owner, a clear reason, a time limit, and confirmation of exactly which data or function the person can access. It should also be fully logged so we can see who approved it, who received it, what they accessed, and when it expired.

context_question: If unauthorized access or data loss is suspected, what immediate response steps would you expect the system or support team to take, and are there any escalation, containment, or notification rules that should apply in those cases?
answer: I’d expect the system to immediately contain the issue by disabling the affected account or access path, preserving logs, and preventing any further changes if possible. Support should escalate right away to security and the appropriate NJIT administrators, and any notification to users or leadership should follow the university’s incident response and privacy rules. If there’s data loss, we’d also want recovery from backup where appropriate, but only after the incident is controlled and the impact is understood.

context_question: Are there any situations where a one-off access exception should be permitted beyond troubleshooting, grading disputes, or urgent administrative needs, and what approval authority, scope limits, and logging would you require in those cases?
answer: Yes, I could see rare cases like accessibility support, compliance reviews, or a temporary research-related need if a course is being used for an approved academic purpose. I’d still want approval from the system owner or a designated dean-level administrator, with the access limited to the smallest necessary scope and a defined expiration time. The access should be logged the same way as any other exception, including the request, approver, timeframe, and what was actually accessed.

context_question: When an incident affects student data or course access, what specific rules should determine who gets notified, what can be shared in those notifications, and whether any communication should wait until privacy or legal review is complete?
answer: Notification should go to the people who need to respond first, like security, IT support, and the relevant NJIT administrator, and then to affected faculty or students only if the incident actually impacts them. We should keep the message minimal at first, sharing only what’s necessary to explain the issue and any required action, without exposing more student data than needed. If there’s any chance the incident involves privacy or legal implications, I’d want the communication reviewed before it goes out to the broader audience.

context_question: For a one-off access exception, are there any situations where the logging needs to capture anything beyond the request, approver, timeframe, and what was accessed—such as the reason for the exception, any conditions attached, or who the log entry should be visible to?
answer: Yes, I’d want the log to include the reason for the exception and any conditions attached, like whether the access was read-only or limited to a single course or student record. It would also be useful to note who is allowed to review that log entry, since some of those details may need to be restricted to security or administrators only. That keeps the audit trail complete without making it broadly visible.

context_question: Who should be permitted to review those log entries, and should any of the visibility differ by role when the entry includes sensitive exception details or student-specific information?
answer: Security staff and authorized system administrators should definitely be able to review them, and I’d also expect audit or compliance personnel to have access when needed. If the entry includes sensitive exception details or student-specific information, then yes, visibility should be tighter by role, so faculty or general support staff would only see what they need for their job. In those cases, the most sensitive parts should be limited to the smallest set of approved reviewers.

context_question: What rules should determine exactly which log details each reviewer role can see when the entry contains sensitive exception information or student-specific data?
answer: I’d base that on least privilege, so each role should only see the details needed to do their job. For example, administrators might see the full audit record, while faculty or support staff could see only a summary or the parts relevant to their case, and student-specific data should be masked unless they are explicitly authorized. If there’s any doubt, the safer default would be to hide the sensitive fields until an approved reviewer needs them.

context_question: When access is granted under one of these exceptions, should the portal make the session strictly read-only, or are there any situations where editing or other actions are still allowed?
answer: In most cases I’d expect those exceptions to be read-only, especially if the access is just for troubleshooting, review, or a temporary lookup. Editing or other actions should only be allowed when the exception was explicitly approved for that purpose, like a grading correction or an administrative update, and even then it should be tightly limited and logged. If it’s not clearly necessary, I’d keep it read-only by default.

context_question: When an incident first has to be communicated, what specific details should the initial notice include versus hold back until later updates, especially if the issue may involve student data, privacy concerns, or legal review?
answer: The initial notice should cover the basic facts: that there is an incident, what part of the portal or course access is affected, who is impacted in general terms, and what immediate steps people should take. It should hold back any detailed student information, technical root-cause speculation, or anything that hasn’t gone through privacy or legal review yet. Later updates can fill in those details once the situation is confirmed and cleared for release.

context_question: When there’s an incident that affects communication features, what immediate notice should instructors or students receive about what’s happening, what they should do next, and what details must stay out of that first message until review is complete?
answer: They should get a short alert saying the communication feature is unavailable or limited, what action they need to take next, like using email or waiting for restoration, and whether any deadlines or class activities are being impacted right away. That first message should not include sensitive student data, internal investigation details, or anything that could be misleading before the issue is fully reviewed. If privacy or legal review is involved, I’d keep the notice very general until they clear it.

context_question: For first-time professors, students, or administrators, are there any specific onboarding or guidance expectations—such as walkthroughs, tooltips, or training—that the portal should provide to reduce the learning curve?
answer: Yes, I’d expect some built-in guidance for first-time users, especially professors and administrators since they’ll be using more of the portal’s features. A short walkthrough or contextual tooltips would be helpful, and for students we’d want simple guidance on joining classes, submitting work, and messaging. I don’t think it needs to be a full training system inside the portal, but it should be easy enough for new users to get started without much help.

context_question: If messaging is slow or temporarily unavailable during normal class activity, what should the portal do with those messages—queue them, retry automatically, alert the sender, or take some other action?
answer: I’d want the portal to retry automatically for a short period and let the sender know that delivery is delayed. If it still can’t go through, it should queue the message so it can be sent once service is restored, rather than dropping it silently. The sender should also get a clear status so they know whether they need to try another channel.

context_question: Are there any limits on that automatic retry and queueing behavior—for example, how long to keep retrying, when queued messages should expire or fail, and whether the sender should be notified differently in each case?
answer: Yes, there should be limits so messages do not sit there indefinitely. I’d expect retries for a short window, and if it still fails after that, the message should either stay queued for a defined period or be marked failed and the sender notified, depending on how critical the message is. The sender should get a different notice when it is still pending versus when it has expired or failed, so they know whether to wait or resend by another method.

context_question: When it comes to post-launch support and maintenance for the virtual learning environment, who should be responsible for handling fixes, updates, and user support after release?
answer: I’d expect NJIT’s IT or LMS support team to own the day-to-day support after release, including user issues, routine fixes, and coordinating updates. The development team would probably handle larger bugs or planned enhancements during the warranty or transition period, but not be the main support contact forever. For professors and students, there should be a clear support path so they know who to contact when something goes wrong.

context_question: When a support issue comes in after launch, what should the escalation path look like for professors and students—what kinds of cases stay with NJIT IT or LMS support, and what kinds should be passed on to the development team or another group?
answer: Routine account, access, password, class enrollment, and how-to questions should stay with NJIT IT or LMS support. Anything that looks like a product defect, data corruption, repeated outage, or a security issue should be escalated to the development team, and anything with privacy or legal implications should also involve the right campus office. If it’s unclear, I’d rather have support triage it first and then pass it along quickly than send users back and forth.

context_question: For support issues that touch privacy, compliance, or institutional policy, what practical rules should determine when NJIT IT or LMS support can resolve the case themselves versus when it must be escalated to a campus office, and who should make that call?
answer: If the issue involves student records, personal data, accessibility, disciplinary concerns, or anything that could violate policy, NJIT IT or LMS support should stop short of making a judgment and escalate it. They can handle the technical side if it is clearly routine, but once there is any real privacy or compliance risk, the campus office that owns that policy area should take over. I’d have support make the initial triage call using a simple checklist, and if there is any doubt, escalate rather than guess.

context_question: When support has to decide whether a case is routine or should be escalated, what practical signs or checklist items should trigger an immediate handoff versus continued troubleshooting on the support side?
answer: Immediate handoff should happen if the case involves unauthorized access, exposure of personal or academic records, suspected cheating or misconduct, or any security incident. It should also be escalated right away if the user is asking for an exception to policy, or if the issue affects multiple users or a critical class function and looks bigger than normal troubleshooting. If it is just a login, navigation, or simple feature issue with no policy or security concern, support can keep working it.

context_question: When support sees one of those higher-risk cases, what specific threshold or evidence should they use to decide it needs an immediate handoff rather than being treated as a normal support ticket?
answer: If there is any clear evidence of data being viewed, changed, or shared by the wrong person, that should be enough for immediate handoff. Also, if the issue has been reproduced more than once, affects more than one account, or suggests a system-wide flaw, support should stop normal troubleshooting and escalate. In practice, I’d rather the threshold be low, because it is better to involve the right office early than to let a sensitive issue linger.
